scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Amis Harvest Festival, also called Ilisin, Malalikid, or Kiloma'an, is a traditional indigenous festival in Taiwan celebrated after the rice harvest, primarily in the Taitung and Hualien regions.
It evolved from earlier millet harvest ceremonies and is held between July and September according to the lunar calendar.
The festival lasts from one to seven days depending on the tribe and includes rituals to honor ancestral gods and pray for future prosperity.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is performed during the Ilisin Harvest Festival to celebrate the harvest, honor ancestors, and ensure future prosperity.
It also serves social functions such as partner selection among youth and the selection of future tribe leaders by elders.
The festival includes rites of passage like the adult ceremony for boys transitioning to manhood.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers form a hand-in-hand circle around elders seated in the center.
Movements include walking, running, and jumping, with coastal tribes performing more complex steps.
A lead singer initiates songs that the group follows.
Watch for Circle Walk, Running Step, Jumping Step.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Participants wear traditional festival clothes, including hats decorated with rooster feathers indicating status.
The dance takes place around a campfire during the festival nights, often under the full moon, creating a communal and ceremonial atmosphere.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The priest plays a central role, overseeing agricultural rituals and communication with the gods.
The priest must be knowledgeable about the calendar, weather, tribal history, dance, and spiritual communication.
The dance movements vary between coastal and mountainous tribes, with coastal dances being more complex.
The Amis harvest dance is a traditional indigenous dance of Taiwan, linked closely to agricultural cycles and ancestral worship.
